questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Views on globalisation
questions.question:
Match List-I (Group) with List-II (View on globalisation).

List-I
(A) Left-wing critics
(B) Right-wing critics, on culture
(C) Advocates of globalisation
(D) Participants in the World Social Forum

List-II
(I) Traditional culture will be harmed and people will lose their age-old ways
(II) Oppose neo-liberal globalisation and seek alternatives
(III) A particular phase of capitalism that makes the rich richer
(IV) Brings greater economic growth, prosperity and openness
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Left critics see globalisation as a phase of capitalism that enriches the few (III). Right-wing critics fear the loss of traditional culture (I). Advocates stress growth and openness (IV). The World Social Forum gathers opponents of neo-liberal globalisation (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the left and right critics. Option (C) gives the advocates' view to the right critics. Option (D) swaps the advocates and the World Social Forum.
Key point: Globalisation is criticised from the left and the right for different reasons.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Visit that began the thaw in India–China relations
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The visit to China by Prime Minister ________ in December 1988 gave new impetus to improving India–China relations.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rajiv Gandhi
Why: Rajiv Gandhi's visit in December 1988 led to steps on confidence-building, cultural exchange and trade.
Why not the others:
(A) Indira Gandhi did not visit China as Prime Minister.
(C) Rao's visit came in 1993.
(D) Vajpayee visited as Foreign Minister in 1979 and as Prime Minister in 2003.
Key point: 1988 began the thaw after the long freeze since 1962.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Prime Ministers of the late 1980s and 1990s and their backing
questions.question:
Match List-I (Prime Minister) with List-II (Government).

List-I
(A) V.P. Singh
(B) H.D. Deve Gowda
(C) Chandra Shekhar
(D) Atal Bihari Vajpayee (from 1998)

List-II
(I) Samajwadi Janata Party government that depended on Congress support
(II) National Democratic Alliance
(III) National Front government
(IV) United Front government
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: V.P. Singh led the National Front (1989–90) (III). Deve Gowda led the United Front (1996–97) (IV). Chandra Shekhar ran a minority government with Congress support (1990–91) (I). Vajpayee led the NDA from 1998 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the National Front and the United Front. Option (B) gives Deve Gowda the Chandra Shekhar government. Option (C) swaps Chandra Shekhar and Vajpayee.
Key point: Minority and coalition governments marked 1989–2004.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Country of the current UN Secretary-General
questions.question: António Guterres, the current Secretary-General of the United Nations, is from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Portugal
Why: António Guterres is a former Prime Minister of Portugal. He became Secretary-General in 2017.
Why not the others:
(B) Spain has not provided a Secretary-General.
(C) Brazil has not provided a Secretary-General.
(D) Austria's Kurt Waldheim held the post in the 1970s.
Key point: The Secretary-General is the UN's chief administrator.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Country that is NOT a member of SAARC
questions.question: Which of the following countries is NOT a member of SAARC?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Myanmar
Why: Myanmar borders India but is not a SAARC member; it is part of ASEAN.
Why not the others:
(A) Afghanistan joined SAARC in 2007.
(B) The Maldives is a founder member.
(C) Bhutan is a founder member.
Key point: SAARC has eight members; Myanmar is in ASEAN.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Civil liberties organisation that emerged around the Emergency
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The experience of the Emergency led to the rise of civil liberties organisations, such as the People's Union for ________ (PUCL).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Civil Liberties
Why: The People's Union for Civil Liberties emerged in this period to defend rights against state excesses.
Why not the others:
(A), (C), (D) The organisation's name is People's Union for Civil Liberties. Democratic Reforms, Human Rights and Electoral Justice are not part of it.
Key point: The Emergency made citizens more aware of civil liberties.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Source of opposition to Valentine's Day celebrations
questions.question: In India, opposition to foreign cultural influences, such as Valentine's Day celebrations and the availability of foreign TV channels, has come mainly from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) right-wing groups
Why: NCERT notes that resistance to foreign cultural influences, such as foreign TV channels and Valentine's Day, has come from the political right.
Why not the others:
(B) Left-wing groups focus on economic issues, such as MNCs and labour.
(C) The WTO promotes trade, not cultural protest.
(D) The Planning Commission was a government body.
Key point: In India, resistance to globalisation comes from both left and right.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Year of the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya
questions.question: In which year was the disputed structure at Ayodhya demolished, in December, leading to communal violence in many parts of the country?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1992
Why: The disputed structure was demolished in December 1992, an event NCERT discusses under the challenge of communalism.
Why not the others:
(A) In 1986 the Faizabad district court ordered the site to be unlocked.
(C) 1990 saw the BJP's rath yatra.
(D) 1989 was a general election year.
Key point: Communalism became a central challenge to secular democracy in the 1990s.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Site of India's first nuclear test
questions.question: In May 1974 India conducted its first nuclear explosion, describing it as a peaceful nuclear explosion. Where was it carried out?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pokhran
Why: The test was conducted at Pokhran, in Rajasthan. India said it would use nuclear power only for peaceful purposes.
Why not the others:
(B) Sriharikota is a satellite launch centre.
(C) Tarapur has India's first nuclear power station.
(D) Kalpakkam is a nuclear research and power site.
Key point: Pokhran 1974 and 1998 are India's test years.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: How the Planning Commission was set up
questions.question: The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by:
options: A) an amendment to the Constitution of India
B) an Act passed by both Houses of Parliament
C) a simple resolution of the Government of India
D) an order of the Supreme Court of India
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) a simple resolution of the Government of India
Why: The Planning Commission was not a constitutional or statutory body. It was set up by a resolution of the Government of India, with the Prime Minister as its chairperson.
Why not the others:
(A) The Constitution does not provide for it.
(B) No Act of Parliament created it.
(D) Courts do not create such bodies.
Key point: A resolution created it; in 2015 the NITI Aayog replaced it.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Who the 'Syndicate' were
questions.question: In Congress politics of the 1960s, the 'Syndicate' referred to:
options: A) a group of big industrialists who funded the Congress party
B) an informal group of senior leaders who controlled the party
C) the alliance of the opposition parties formed for the 1971 polls
D) the committee of cabinet ministers in charge of national planning
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) an informal group of senior leaders who controlled the party
Why: The Syndicate was a group of senior Congress leaders, including Kamaraj, S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa and Atulya Ghosh, who controlled the party organisation.
Why not the others:
(A) They were party leaders, not industrialists.
(C) The opposition alliance of 1971 was called the 'grand alliance'.
(D) It was not a government body.
Key point: Indira Gandhi's clash with the Syndicate led to the 1969 split.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: India's traditional source of military hardware
questions.question: Which country has historically been India's largest supplier of military hardware?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Russia
Why: Most of India's military hardware has come from the Soviet Union and then Russia, a key part of their strategic partnership.
Why not the others:
(A) France has supplied some aircraft but is not the largest source.
(C) Israel is a newer supplier.
(D) The US became a supplier much later.
Key point: Defence ties anchor the India–Russia relationship.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Leaders in the Congress crisis of the 1960s
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Role).

List-I
(A) K. Kamaraj
(B) Ram Manohar Lohia
(C) V.V. Giri
(D) N. Sanjeeva Reddy

List-II
(I) Gave the strategy of non-Congressism
(II) Won the 1969 presidential election as an independent candidate
(III) Official Congress candidate for President in 1969
(IV) Congress President who played a key role in choosing Prime Ministers after Nehru
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: As Congress President, Kamaraj guided the choice of Shastri and then Indira Gandhi (IV). Lohia argued that the opposition must unite against the Congress (I). V.V. Giri, backed by Indira Gandhi, won as an independent (II). Sanjeeva Reddy was the Syndicate-backed official candidate (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Giri and Reddy. Option (B) swaps Kamaraj and Lohia. Option (D) gives non-Congressism to Giri.
Key point: The 1969 presidential contest split the Congress.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Which was NOT a trend of the coalition era
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a feature of Indian politics in the coalition era after 1989?
options: A) The end of the Congress's dominance
B) The growing political weight of the backward castes
C) A wide agreement among major parties on the new economic policies
D) A decline in the role of regional parties at the Centre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A decline in the role of regional parties at the Centre
Why: The role of regional parties grew, not declined. Many of them became partners in coalition governments at the Centre.
Why not the others:
(A) The Congress lost its dominance after 1989.
(B) OBC politics rose sharply after Mandal.
(C) Most parties came to accept the new economic policies.
Key point: Coalitions gave regional parties a share of national power.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Founder of the DMK
questions.question: The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), which grew out of the Dravidian movement, was founded in 1949 by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C.N. Annadurai
Why: C.N. Annadurai broke away from Periyar's Dravidar Kazhagam and founded the DMK in 1949.
Why not the others:
(A) Periyar founded the Dravidar Kazhagam.
(B) Kamaraj was a Congress leader.
(D) Karunanidhi led the DMK later.
Key point: The Dravidian movement turned into a strong regional party.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Dalit and backward-class politics and economic reform in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) Formation of the Bahujan Samaj Party
(B) Formation of BAMCEF
(C) Launch of the New Economic Policy
(D) The decision to implement the Mandal Commission's recommendations
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Why: (B) BAMCEF was formed in 1978. (A) Kanshi Ram founded the BSP in 1984. (D) The National Front decided to implement Mandal in August 1990. (C) The New Economic Policy was launched in 1991.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts the BSP before BAMCEF. Option (C) puts Mandal before the BSP. Option (D) puts the economic reforms before Mandal.
Key point: BAMCEF built the base on which the BSP grew.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Groups inside the Congress in its dominant phase
questions.question: Fill in the blank: In the era of one-party dominance, groups inside the Congress based on ideology or personal ambition were known as ________; the party tolerated and even encouraged them.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) factions
Why: NCERT calls these groups factions. Rather than leaving the party, they stayed in it and competed with one another, which made the Congress a coalition.
Why not the others:
(A) "Wings" is not the term NCERT uses.
(B) "Cells" describes cadre parties, such as the Communists.
(C) "The Syndicate" was a specific group of Congress leaders in the 1960s.
Key point: Factions let the Congress hold many interests together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: The United Nations and its Security Council — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The United Nations was founded in 1945, after the Second World War.
(B) The five permanent members of the Security Council have a veto.
(C) In the General Assembly each member state has one vote.
(D) India has been a permanent member of the Security Council since 2010.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the UN was founded in 1945. (B) the US, Russia, the UK, France and China hold a veto. (C) every member has one vote in the General Assembly.
Why not the others: (D) is false: India is not a permanent member; it has served as an elected non-permanent member, for example in 2011–12. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: India seeks a permanent seat but does not hold one.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of balance of power
questions.question: In traditional security, 'balance of power' refers to:
options: A) keeping power distributed so that no rival becomes dominant
B) an agreement among states to destroy all their weapons
C) the control of every national army by the United Nations
D) giving equal votes to all states in the General Assembly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) keeping power distributed so that no rival becomes dominant
Why: Under the balance of power, states watch and match the power of rivals, through their own build-up or alliances, so that no state becomes dominant.
Why not the others:
(B) Destroying weapons is disarmament.
(C) The UN has no such control.
(D) One country one vote is about the General Assembly, not power balance.
Key point: Balance of power is a traditional way of keeping security.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Example of a non-traditional threat
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a non-traditional threat to security?
options: A) An invasion by the army of a neighbour
B) A naval blockade imposed by a rival state
C) The spread of epidemics such as HIV-AIDS
D) A military alliance of hostile states
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The spread of epidemics such as HIV-AIDS
Why: Epidemics such as HIV-AIDS, bird flu and SARS spread across borders and threaten human life, which makes them non-traditional threats.
Why not the others:
(A) An invasion is a traditional military threat.
(B) A blockade is a military action by a state.
(D) Hostile alliances are a traditional security concern.
Key point: Disease is a threat to people, not to state borders.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Why democracy has struggled in Pakistan
questions.question: According to NCERT, why has democracy failed to take stable root in Pakistan?
options: A) Pakistan has never held a general election since it became independent.
B) The army, the clergy and landowning elites have dominated its politics.
C) The constitution of Pakistan has banned all political parties for good.
D) The United Nations has kept civilian leaders from ruling Pakistan.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The army, the clergy and landowning elites have dominated its politics.
Why: NCERT points to the dominance of the army, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy, as well as conflict with India, which has strengthened pro-military groups.
Why not the others:
(A) Pakistan has held many elections.
(C) Political parties are not banned.
(D) The UN has played no such role.
Key point: Military rule has alternated with elected governments in Pakistan.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: The European Union — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The European Union has its own flag, anthem, founding date and currency.
(B) The Euro is the common currency of many EU members.
(C) The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Economic Community.
(D) The EU grew out of the European Economic Community formed in 1957.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the European Economic Community was created in 1957. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 established the European Union.
Why not the others: (A) the EU has many symbols of a state. (B) the Euro is used across much of the EU. (D) the EEC of 1957 was the EU's forerunner. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: EEC 1957 → EU 1992.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Leader who handled the integration of princely states
questions.question: Who, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, played the leading role in integrating the princely states into India?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Why: Sardar Patel led the negotiations, using persuasion and firmness, that brought most princely states into the Indian Union.
Why not the others:
(A) Nehru was Prime Minister and handled foreign affairs.
(B) Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.
(C) Azad was Education Minister.
Key point: Patel is remembered as the architect of integration.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Result of the 2014 Lok Sabha election
questions.question: What was the significance of the 2014 Lok Sabha election?
options: A) The Congress won a majority on its own for the first time since 1984.
B) A single party, the BJP, won a majority on its own for the first time since 1984.
C) No party or alliance won a majority, and a minority government was formed.
D) The Janata Dal returned to power at the Centre.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A single party, the BJP, won a majority on its own for the first time since 1984.
Why: In 2014 the BJP won a majority of Lok Sabha seats on its own, the first single-party majority since the Congress victory of 1984. It governed as part of the NDA.
Why not the others:
(A) The Congress lost heavily in 2014.
(C) The NDA had a clear majority.
(D) The Janata Dal had broken up long before.
Key point: 2014 ended the long run of hung Parliaments from 1989.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: The idea of a 'minimalist state'
questions.question: Under globalisation, the old welfare state is said to give way to a more 'minimalist state'. This means a state that:
options: A) gives up its armed forces and depends on its allies
B) stops holding elections and rules through officials
C) withdraws from welfare and leaves more to the market
D) hands over parts of its territory to multinationals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) withdraws from welfare and leaves more to the market
Why: Globalisation has eroded state capacity. The welfare state gives way to a minimalist state that performs core functions, such as law and order and security, and withdraws from many welfare functions.
Why not the others:
(A) The state keeps its armed forces.
(B) Elections continue.
(D) The state keeps its territory and sovereignty.
Key point: The market, not the state, becomes the main decider of priorities.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Leader of the Naga National Council
questions.question: The Naga National Council, which declared independence for Nagaland and led an armed struggle, was led by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Angami Zapu Phizo
Why: A.Z. Phizo led the Naga National Council's demand for independence from 1951.
Why not the others:
(B) Laldenga led the Mizo National Front.
(C) Prafulla Kumar Mahanta led the Assam movement and became Chief Minister.
(D) Bodhachandra Singh was the Maharaja of Manipur.
Key point: Phizo is to Nagaland what Laldenga is to Mizoram.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: The first general elections and the Election Commission — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Election Commission of India was set up in January 1950.
(B) Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner.
(C) In the first general election, each candidate had a separate ballot box with his or her symbol on it.
(D) Electronic voting machines were used throughout the country from the 1952 election onwards.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the Commission was set up in January 1950. (B) Sukumar Sen was its first head. (C) voters dropped their blank ballot paper into the box of the candidate they chose.
Why not the others: (D) is false: EVMs came much later, and were used across the whole country only from the 2004 election. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: From separate boxes in 1952 to EVMs everywhere in 2004.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Why the 1971 'grand alliance' failed
questions.question: Why did the 'grand alliance' of non-Communist, non-Congress parties fail against Indira Gandhi's Congress in 1971?
options: A) It refused to contest the election and called for a boycott instead.
B) It had the support of the Syndicate only in the southern States.
C) It was banned by the Election Commission during the campaign.
D) It lacked a positive programme, while Indira offered 'Garibi Hatao'.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It lacked a positive programme, while Indira offered 'Garibi Hatao'.
Why: The alliance's main slogan was 'Indira Hatao'. Indira Gandhi offered a positive programme, 'Garibi Hatao', backed by bank nationalisation and the abolition of privy purses.
Why not the others:
(A) The alliance did contest the election.
(B) Its weakness was not regional support.
(C) No party was banned in 1971.
Key point: A clear positive slogan beat a purely negative one.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Founder of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh
questions.question: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951. Who was its founder-President?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
Why: Shyama Prasad Mukherjee founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh in 1951 and was its first President.
Why not the others:
(B) Deen Dayal Upadhyaya was a later leader and ideologue of the party.
(C) Balraj Madhok was another early leader.
(D) Vajpayee was a younger leader who later led the BJP.
Key point: The Jana Sangh stood for 'one country, one culture and one nation'.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Terms of the Soviet system and its end
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Perestroika
(B) 'Second World'
(C) Shock therapy
(D) Warsaw Pact

List-II
(I) Military alliance of the Soviet-bloc states
(II) Restructuring of the Soviet economy and system
(III) A sudden move to a capitalist economy after communism
(IV) The bloc of socialist countries of Eastern Europe led by the USSR
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Perestroika means restructuring (II). The 'Second World' was the socialist bloc led by the USSR (IV). Shock therapy was the rapid move to capitalism (III). The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet bloc's military alliance (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Perestroika and the Second World. Option (B) swaps shock therapy and the Warsaw Pact. Option (D) swaps the Second World and shock therapy.
Key point: Perestroika reformed the system; shock therapy replaced it.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: What the 'Kerala model' of development stressed
questions.question: The 'Kerala model' of development is known for its emphasis on:
options: A) heavy industry, large dams and a strong state sector
B) education, health, land reform and food distribution
C) rapid privatisation and large-scale foreign investment
D) the export of cash crops and plantation farm products
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) education, health, land reform and food distribution
Why: Kerala stressed education, health, land reform, effective food distribution and poverty alleviation, achieving high human development despite low per capita income.
Why not the others:
(A) Heavy industry was the thrust of the national Second Plan.
(C) Privatisation is linked with the post-1991 reforms.
(D) Kerala's model was not export-led farming.
Key point: Kerala showed that social indicators can rise without high incomes.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: First non-Congress Prime Minister of India
questions.question: After the 1977 elections, the first non-Congress Prime Minister of India was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Morarji Desai
Why: The Janata Party won the 1977 election, and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister.
Why not the others:
(A) Charan Singh followed Desai in 1979.
(B) Jagjivan Ram was a contender but did not become Prime Minister.
(D) JP led the movement but held no office.
Key point: 1977 ended thirty years of Congress rule at the Centre.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: New States created after the 1956 reorganisation
questions.question:
Match List-I (State) with List-II (Year of creation).

List-I
(A) Nagaland
(B) Gujarat
(C) Haryana
(D) Meghalaya

List-II
(I) 1972
(II) 1963
(III) 1960
(IV) 1966
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Nagaland became a State in 1963 (II). Gujarat was carved out of Bombay State in 1960 (III). Haryana was separated from Punjab in 1966 (IV). Meghalaya was carved out of Assam in 1972 (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Nagaland and Gujarat. Option (C) swaps Gujarat and Haryana. Option (D) swaps Haryana and Meghalaya.
Key point: Reorganisation went on through the 1960s and 1970s.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Leaders and groups of South Asian countries
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader or group) with List-II (Country).

List-I
(A) Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman
(B) Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
(C) King Gyanendra
(D) LTTE

List-II
(I) Nepal
(II) Sri Lanka
(III) Pakistan
(IV) Bangladesh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Mujib led Bangladesh's freedom struggle and became its first leader (IV). Bhutto led Pakistan after 1971 (III). King Gyanendra seized full power in Nepal in 2005 (I). The LTTE fought for a separate Tamil state in Sri Lanka (II).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps Mujib and Bhutto. Option (C) swaps Nepal and Sri Lanka. Option (D) puts Bhutto in Nepal.
Key point: Each country took a different path between democracy and conflict.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Regions of Russia with violent secessionist movements
questions.question: Which two regions of Russia saw violent secessionist movements after the Soviet Union broke up?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chechnya and Dagestan
Why: Chechnya and Dagestan, within the Russian Federation, saw violent secessionist movements, and Moscow's military response was criticised.
Why not the others:
(B) Belarus and Ukraine became independent states, not regions of Russia.
(C) Latvia and Estonia are independent Baltic states.
(D) Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan are independent Central Asian states.
Key point: Conflict continued inside Russia after 1991.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Principle on which the territories of the two countries were divided
questions.question: At Partition, on what principle was it decided which areas would go to Pakistan?
options: A) Areas with a Muslim majority would make up Pakistan.
B) Areas with an Urdu-speaking majority would make up Pakistan.
C) The areas that voted in a plebiscite in 1947 would go to Pakistan.
D) All the princely states west of the Indus would go to Pakistan.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Areas with a Muslim majority would make up Pakistan.
Why: The principle was religious majorities: areas where Muslims were a majority would form Pakistan, and the rest would stay with India.
Why not the others:
(B) Language was not the basis; Bengal and Punjab were split on religion.
(C) There was no general plebiscite in 1947.
(D) Princely states were free to choose; geography west of the Indus was not the rule.
Key point: Religion, not language, decided the lines of Partition.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Traditional and non-traditional security — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In the traditional view, the greatest danger to a country comes from military threats.
(B) Terrorism is a traditional security threat, because it is always carried out by the army of another state.
(C) Global poverty is a source of insecurity in the non-traditional view.
(D) Deterrence and defence are ways of meeting threats in the traditional view.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: terrorism is a non-traditional threat, involving political violence that targets civilians, usually by groups rather than state armies.
Why not the others: (A) the traditional view centres on military threats to the state. (C) poverty creates insecurity for people. (D) deterrence prevents war; defence limits it. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Non-traditional threats go beyond armies and states.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Zones that attracted foreign investment to China
questions.question: China's post-1978 reforms attracted foreign investors to specially created areas with special rules. These are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Special Economic Zones
Why: China set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) where foreign investors could set up enterprises under special rules.
Why not the others:
(A) Free Trade Agreements are treaties between countries.
(B) Collective farms were part of the earlier, Maoist system.
(C) Treaty ports were a nineteenth-century colonial arrangement.
Key point: SEZs were central to China's rise.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: North-East statehood and accords in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The Assam Accord
(B) Nagaland becomes a State
(C) Sikkim becomes a State of India
(D) Mizoram becomes a State
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C), (A), (D)
Why: (B) Nagaland became a State in 1963. (C) Sikkim became India's 22nd State in 1975. (A) The Assam Accord was signed in 1985. (D) Mizoram became a State in 1987.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the Assam Accord before Sikkim. Option (B) puts Sikkim before Nagaland. Option (C) puts Mizoram before the Assam Accord.
Key point: 1963 → 1975 → 1985 → 1987.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Non-alignment and relations with China — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held at Belgrade in 1961.
(B) The Dalai Lama sought and got political asylum in India in 1962.
(C) Panchsheel included the principle of peaceful coexistence.
(D) Non-alignment did not mean staying away from world affairs.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: the Dalai Lama crossed into India and was given asylum in 1959, three years before the war.
Why not the others: (A) Belgrade hosted the first NAM summit in 1961. (C) peaceful coexistence was one of the five principles. (D) NAM members took active positions on world issues; they only stayed out of the two Cold War blocs. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Tibet in 1959 strained India–China ties before 1962.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Mediator of the Tashkent Agreement
questions.question: The Tashkent Agreement of 1966 between Lal Bahadur Shastri and Ayub Khan was mediated by:
options: C) British Prime Minister Harold Wilson
D) Soviet Prime Minister Alexei Kosygin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Soviet Prime Minister Alexei Kosygin
Why: The Soviet Prime Minister, Alexei Kosygin, brought the two leaders together at Tashkent in January 1966.
Why not the others:
(A) The US did not mediate at Tashkent.
(B) U Thant was involved in UN ceasefire calls, not the agreement.
(C) Britain did not host or mediate it.
Key point: The Soviet Union mediated the end of the 1965 war.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: The crisis before the Emergency — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In 1974 students in Gujarat started an agitation that came to be called the Navnirman movement.
(B) Jayaprakash Narayan called for a 'Total Revolution'.
(C) In 1973 three senior judges were superseded in the appointment of the Chief Justice of India.
(D) The nationwide railway strike of 1974 was led by Charan Singh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the Navnirman movement began in Gujarat in January 1974. (B) JP called for 'Total Revolution' to bring about change in every sphere. (C) A.N. Ray's appointment in 1973 superseded three senior judges.
Why not the others: (D) is false: George Fernandes, the socialist trade union leader, led the 1974 railway strike. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Protests, the strike and the judges' issue all came before June 1975.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: From the Berlin Wall to Gorbachev's reforms in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) Gorbachev becomes General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party
(B) The unification of Germany
(C) The building of the Berlin Wall
(D) Soviet intervention in Afghanistan
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) The Berlin Wall was built in 1961. (D) Soviet troops entered Afghanistan in 1979. (A) Gorbachev took over in 1985. (B) Germany was unified in October 1990.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Afghanistan before the Wall. Option (B) puts Gorbachev before Afghanistan. Option (C) puts German unification before Gorbachev.
Key point: The Wall rose in 1961, fell in 1989, and Germany reunited in 1990.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: What the WTO succeeded
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The World Trade Organisation, set up in 1995, succeeded the ________, which had governed world trade since the end of the Second World War.
options: C) United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
D) General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs
Why: The WTO succeeded the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT), created after the Second World War.
Why not the others:
(A) The IMF handles finance, not trade rules.
(B) Bretton Woods was a conference, not a trade body.
(C) UNCTAD is a UN body that still exists.
Key point: GATT became the WTO in 1995.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: South Asian milestones in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The SAFTA agreement comes into force
(B) Bangladesh becomes independent
(C) SAARC is set up
(D) Pakistan conducts nuclear tests
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C), (D), (A)
Why: (B) Bangladesh became independent in 1971. (C) SAARC was set up in 1985. (D) Pakistan tested nuclear devices in May 1998. (A) SAFTA came into force in 2006.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts SAARC before Bangladesh. Option (B) puts the nuclear tests before SAARC. Option (D) puts SAFTA before the tests.
Key point: 1971 → 1985 → 1998 → 2006.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Which of the following is NOT a global common
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Some parts of the world lie outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state. They are called the global commons, and they include the earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor beyond national waters and outer space. Because no single state controls them, they can be managed only through international cooperation. That cooperation has produced landmark agreements: a treaty that reserves Antarctica for peaceful and scientific use, a protocol to protect the ozone layer, and later an environmental protocol for the Antarctic region. Yet agreement is hard to reach. Scientific knowledge about problems such as ozone depletion is often uncertain and disputed, and the benefits of exploiting the commons depend heavily on technology, which the industrialised North has and the developing South largely lacks. Below the global level, many communities manage resources collectively. A common property resource is owned and used by a group whose members have both rights and duties regarding its care. Customary rules and mutual understanding, rather than the market or the state, keep such resources alive, though privatisation, rising population and the pressure of the market have weakened many of these arrangements.

Question: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT a global common?
options: A) The earth's atmosphere above all states
B) Antarctica and its surrounding region
C) Outer space beyond the atmosphere
D) A forest managed by a village community
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A forest managed by a village community
Why: A forest managed by a village community is a common property resource, owned and governed by a group. A global common lies outside the jurisdiction of every state.
Why not the others:
(A) The atmosphere is named in the passage as a global common.
(B) Antarctica is named as a global common.
(C) Outer space is named as a global common.
Key point: Global commons belong to no state; common property belongs to a community.

questions.sub_topic: Protocol that protects the ozone layer

Question: The passage mentions a protocol to protect the ozone layer. Which agreement is this?
options: C) The Antarctic Environmental Protocol of 1991
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Montreal Protocol of 1987
Why: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 limits the production of ozone-depleting substances, such as chlorofluorocarbons.
Why not the others:
(A) The Kyoto Protocol deals with greenhouse gas emissions.
(C) The 1991 protocol concerns environmental protection in Antarctica.
(D) The Rio Declaration set out principles for environment and development.
Key point: Montreal is for the ozone layer; Kyoto is for greenhouse gases.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why cooperation over the global commons is difficult
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Some parts of the world lie outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state. They are called the global commons, and they include the earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor beyond national waters and outer space. Because no single state controls them, they can be managed only through international cooperation. That cooperation has produced landmark agreements: a treaty that reserves Antarctica for peaceful and scientific use, a protocol to protect the ozone layer, and later an environmental protocol for the Antarctic region. Yet agreement is hard to reach. Below the global level, many communities manage resources collectively. A common property resource is owned and used by a group whose members have both rights and duties regarding its care. Customary rules and mutual understanding, rather than the market or the state, keep such resources alive, though privatisation, rising population and the pressure of the market have weakened many of these arrangements.

Question: Based on the passage, which of the following best explains why it is hard to reach agreement on managing the global commons?
options: A) The global commons already belong to the industrialised countries of the North.
B) Local communities refuse to share their customary rules with national governments.
C) Science is disputed, and gains from the commons depend on technology the North has.
D) The United Nations has no power at all to discuss questions of the environment.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Science is disputed, and gains from the commons depend on technology the North has.
Why: The passage gives two reasons: uncertain and contested science (as with the ozone hole), and unequal technology, which lets the developed North profit more from the commons than the South.
Why not the others:
(A) The commons, by definition, are owned by no state.
(B) Customary rules concern common property, not the global commons.
(D) The UN has hosted major environmental conferences, such as Rio in 1992.
Key point: The North–South gap shapes every debate on the commons.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Outer space and the North–South divide
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Some parts of the world lie outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state. They are called the global commons, and they include the earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor beyond national waters and outer space. Because no single state controls them, they can be managed only through international cooperation. That cooperation has produced landmark agreements: a treaty that reserves Antarctica for peaceful and scientific use, a protocol to protect the ozone layer, and later an environmental protocol for the Antarctic region. Yet agreement is hard to reach. Scientific knowledge about problems such as ozone depletion is often uncertain and disputed, and the benefits of exploiting the commons depend heavily on technology, which the industrialised North has and the developing South largely lacks. Below the global level, many communities manage resources collectively. A common property resource is owned and used by a group whose members have both rights and duties regarding its care. Customary rules and mutual understanding, rather than the market or the state, keep such resources alive, though privatisation, rising population and the pressure of the market have weakened many of these arrangements.

Question: Applying the passage's argument to outer space, which statement is most accurate?
options: A) Though it belongs to no state, countries with advanced technology gain far more from it.
B) It is a common property resource that national space agencies own and manage jointly.
C) Developing countries benefit more from it, because they have launched fewer satellites.
D) It needs no international cooperation, because no country is yet able to reach it.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Though it belongs to no state, countries with advanced technology gain far more from it.
Why: Like the other commons, outer space is outside every state's jurisdiction, but the benefits of using it depend on technology. That gives the industrialised North a large advantage.
Why not the others:
(B) Space is a global common, not property of a community or agency.
(C) The passage says benefits follow technology, which the South largely lacks.
(D) Several countries do reach space, which is why cooperation is needed.
Key point: Equal ownership does not mean equal benefit.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Who keeps common property resources alive
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Some parts of the world lie outside the sovereign jurisdiction of any one state. They are called the global commons, and they include the earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, the ocean floor beyond national waters and outer space. Because no single state controls them, they can be managed only through international cooperation. Yet agreement is hard to reach. Customary rules and mutual understanding, rather than the market or the state, keep such resources alive, though privatisation, rising population and the pressure of the market have weakened many of these arrangements.

Question: According to the passage, a common property resource is kept alive mainly by:
options: A) the market, through private ownership by individual members
B) international treaties signed among the states of the region
C) the environmental loans given by the World Bank to the village
D) the customary rules and mutual understanding of its community
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the customary rules and mutual understanding of its community
Why: The passage says common property is owned by a group whose members have rights and duties, and that custom and mutual understanding, not the market or the state, sustain it.
Why not the others:
(A) Privatisation is named as one of the pressures that weaken common property.
(B) Treaties among states govern the global commons, not community property.
(C) The passage does not mention the World Bank.
Key point: Community norms, not markets, govern common property.
